title: Identifiability of Child's Location Data
description: Live GPS coordinates transmitted from the child's device are inherently identifiable to the specific child, enabling direct identification of the individual through location data.
assumptions: GPS data is transmitted without sufficient anonymization or pseudonymization measures.

title: Linkability of Location Data Across Time
description: Regular GPS transmissions enable linking of location data across time periods, allowing reconstruction of the child's movement patterns, routines, and potentially sensitive locations (e.g., school, home, medical facilities).
assumptions: Data is stored and accessible for analysis over time.

title: Excessive Data Collection via Continuous GPS Tracking
description: Live GPS coordinates transmitted at regular intervals may exceed data minimization principles, collecting more precise and frequent location data than necessary for the stated purpose.
assumptions: The stated purpose does not require continuous real-time location tracking.

title: Unauthorized Use of Location Data for Tracking
description: The backend process may use the collected GPS data for purposes beyond the original intent, such as unauthorized tracking, profiling, or sharing with third parties.
assumptions: The backend has capabilities to repurpose the data without proper consent mechanisms.

title: Non-compliance with Location Data Regulations
description: Collection and processing of child's GPS location data may violate GDPR and other privacy regulations requiring explicit consent, data minimization, and purpose limitation for sensitive location data.
assumptions: Regulatory requirements for location data processing are not fully met.

title: Unnecessary Location Data Collection and Storage
description: The backend writes each location ping to the Location History Store, potentially collecting and storing more location data than strictly necessary for the app's functionality. This violates the minimality principle of data disclosure.
assumptions: Location data is personal data that can identify individuals through movement patterns. The app may not need to store all location pings long-term.
uncertainty_note: Using Dd.1.1 based on context [5] about data disclosure and minimality principle. The exact tree node may vary by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: Linkability of Location History to Individual Identity
description: The stored location history can be linked to identify specific users, especially when combined with other data sources. Movement patterns are highly identifying.
assumptions: Location data combined with timestamps can create a unique profile for each user, potentially revealing sensitive information about their habits, routines, and whereabouts.
uncertainty_note: Using L.1.1 as a reasonable node for linkability threats in location data contexts.

title: Inference of Sensitive Information from Location Patterns
description: Analysis of location history can reveal sensitive information such as home address, workplace, religious sites, medical facilities, or political activities through pattern recognition.
assumptions: Location patterns over time can be analyzed to infer sensitive personal information beyond what was explicitly collected.
uncertainty_note: Using I.1.1 as a reasonable node for inference threats in location data contexts.

title: Linkability of Geofencing Notifications
description: The geofencing engine could link multiple arrival/departure notifications to the same user, enabling reconstruction of movement patterns and location history.
assumptions: Notifications are associated with identifiable user accounts and timestamps are precise enough to correlate movements.

title: Identification via Geofencing Alerts
description: Arrival/departure notifications could be used to identify the user's presence at specific locations, potentially revealing sensitive activities or routines.
assumptions: Notifications contain or can be correlated with user identifiers, and the external entity has access to this data.

title: Disclosure of Location Data to External Entity
description: Geofencing notifications containing location information could be disclosed to unauthorized parties if the external entity (EE1) is compromised or if data is transmitted insecurely.
assumptions: The external entity has access to the notification data and may not have adequate security controls.

title: Non-compliance with Privacy Regulations
description: Sharing geofencing location data with an external entity may violate GDPR or other privacy regulations if proper consent mechanisms and data minimization principles are not followed.
assumptions: The data transfer involves personal data (location) and may not have explicit user consent or legal basis.
uncertainty_note: Regulatory requirements vary by jurisdiction; this is a general concern.

title: Parent identity linked to child profile data
description: The parent's identity can be linked to the child's personal information (name, DOB, school) and geofence zones through the registration process, potentially enabling tracking of the child's location and activities via the parent's account.
assumptions: The system stores parent-child relationship data that can be used to link identities across data flows.

title: Child's personal data disclosed to unauthorized parties
description: The child's sensitive personal information (name, DOB, school) and geofence zones could be disclosed to unauthorized third parties through the registration flow, violating privacy expectations for minors.
assumptions: The system may have inadequate access controls or data sharing policies for child-related data.

title: Unauthorized account creation or profile manipulation
description: An unauthorized actor could usurp the parent's identity to create false child profiles or manipulate geofence zones, potentially leading to stalking or safety concerns.
assumptions: The authentication mechanism may be insufficient to verify the true parent-child relationship.

title: Geofence zone data exposed during processing
description: The Mobile App Backend (P1) may expose geofence zone data during processing, potentially revealing the child's home/school locations to unauthorized parties or through system vulnerabilities.
assumptions: The process may log or transmit geofence data without proper encryption or access controls.

title: Non-compliance with children's privacy regulations
description: The system may fail to comply with privacy regulations (e.g., COPPA, GDPR-K) regarding collection and processing of children's personal data during the registration flow.
assumptions: The system may not have adequate consent mechanisms or data minimization practices for child data.

title: Excessive Personal Data Storage in Backend
description: The Mobile App Backend (P1) stores comprehensive family account, child profile, and geofence zone data in DS2. This represents explicit data disclosure by design. The minimality principle requires that only strictly required personal data be stored. Storing full child profiles and geofence data may exceed what's necessary for the intended functionality, creating avoidable disclosure risk.
assumptions: The system stores more detailed personal data than minimally required for account management and geofencing functionality.
uncertainty_note: Tree node Dd.1.1 is inferred from context about data disclosure; exact LINDDUN Pro node may vary.

title: Unauthorized Access to Stored Family Data
description: The backend (P1) stores sensitive family account and child profile data in DS2. If access controls are inadequate, unauthorized parties could access or manipulate this stored data, leading to privacy violations. This is a usurpation threat where legitimate users or systems could be bypassed.
assumptions: Access controls to the backend and data store may not be sufficiently restrictive.
uncertainty_note: Tree node U.1.1 is inferred; exact LINDDUN Pro node may vary.

title: Data Integrity Risk for Stored Profile Information
description: The backend (P1) stores child profile and geofence zone data in DS2. If data integrity controls are weak, this information could be tampered with, leading to incorrect geofence boundaries or inaccurate child profile data. This could have safety implications for geofencing functionality.
assumptions: Data integrity mechanisms may not be fully implemented or enforced.
uncertainty_note: Tree node D.1.1 is inferred; exact LINDDUN Pro node may vary.

title: Unauthorized Location Data Disclosure
description: Parent (EE1) may request and receive child's location or location history data without proper authorization or consent, leading to potential privacy violations.
assumptions: Parent has access to child's location data without explicit consent or legal basis
uncertainty_note: Using D.1.1 as it represents disclosure threats at source/flow/data positions

title: Location Data Linkability to Child
description: Mobile App Backend (P1) processes location data that can be linked to the specific child, enabling tracking of movements and activities.
assumptions: Location data contains sufficient granularity to identify the child's movements
uncertainty_note: Using L.1.1 as it represents linkability threats at source/flow/data positions

title: Child Identifiability from Location History
description: Mobile App Backend (P1) stores and processes location history that can identify the child's identity, habits, and routines.
assumptions: Location history data patterns can be used to identify the child
uncertainty_note: Using I.1.1 as it represents identifiability threats at source/flow/data positions

title: Regulatory Non-Compliance for Location Data Processing
description: Mobile App Backend (P1) may process child's location data without proper legal basis, violating GDPR or similar privacy regulations regarding children's data.
assumptions: Location data of children requires special protection under privacy regulations
uncertainty_note: Using Nc.1.1 as it represents non-compliance threats at source/flow/data positions

title: Identifiability of Location History Data
description: Location history data retrieved from the store can be directly linked to a specific individual, enabling identification of the user's movements and patterns.
assumptions: The location history contains sufficient granularity (timestamps, coordinates) to identify the user.

title: Unauthorized Disclosure of Location History
description: Stored location history may be accessed by unauthorized parties or disclosed beyond intended recipients during retrieval by the backend.
assumptions: Access controls on the data store may be insufficient or compromised.

title: Linkability of Location Data to Other User Data
description: Location history retrieved by the backend can be linked to other personal data (e.g., user profile, device ID, other services) to create comprehensive user profiles.
assumptions: The backend has access to or can correlate with other user data sources.

title: Regulatory Non-Compliance in Location Data Handling
description: Retrieval and display of location history may violate privacy regulations (e.g., GDPR, CCPA) regarding consent, data minimization, or purpose limitation.
assumptions: The system may not have proper consent mechanisms or data retention policies for location data.

title: Parent identity linked with child location data
description: When the parent initiates the invitation, their identity becomes linked with the child's location data being shared, creating a privacy risk that the parent's association with the child's location can be traced.
assumptions: The system records which parent initiated the invitation and links this to the location data being shared.

title: Parent identifiable through invitation action
description: The parent's identity is directly identifiable when they perform the invitation action to share the child's location with a secondary guardian.
assumptions: The system requires parent authentication and records their identity when initiating the location sharing.

title: Child location disclosed to unauthorized secondary guardian
description: The mobile app backend may disclose the child's location to a secondary guardian who was not properly authorized or whose authorization was not verified.
assumptions: The system may have insufficient authorization checks when granting location access to secondary guardians.

title: Excessive location data retained for secondary guardian access
description: The mobile app backend may retain more location data than necessary for the secondary guardian's viewing access, violating data minimization principles.
assumptions: The system stores historical location data beyond what is needed for the secondary guardian to view current location.

title: Secondary guardian account compromised enabling location access
description: If the secondary guardian's account credentials are compromised, an attacker could gain unauthorized access to the child's location data through the mobile app backend.
assumptions: The secondary guardian's account security is not sufficiently protected, and the system does not have adequate monitoring for suspicious access patterns.

title: Unauthorized disclosure of child's live location to unauthorized parties
description: The backend shares the child's live location with the secondary guardian, but if the guardian's access credentials are compromised or the guardian shares the data further, the location information could be disclosed to unauthorized third parties.
assumptions: The guardian may have access to the data beyond their intended scope, or the data could be intercepted during transmission.

title: Linkability of location data with other child information
description: The secondary guardian could potentially link the live location data with other information they have about the child (e.g., schedule, activities, other data sources), creating a more detailed profile of the child's movements and habits.
assumptions: The guardian has access to other data sources about the child that could be correlated with the location data.

title: Usurpation of location data access by unauthorized actors
description: If the secondary guardian's account is compromised or credentials are stolen, an unauthorized actor could access the child's live location data, potentially tracking the child's movements without proper authorization.
assumptions: The guardian's authentication mechanism may be vulnerable to credential theft or account takeover.

title: Data degradation of live location during transmission
description: The live location data may lose precision or accuracy during transmission from the backend to the secondary guardian, potentially resulting in less accurate location information than intended.
assumptions: Network conditions, compression, or processing may degrade the location data quality.

title: Unauthorized Disclosure to Third Parties
description: Advertising/analytics partner may share or sell the aggregated analytics data to additional third parties beyond the original agreement, exposing user engagement patterns to unauthorized entities.
assumptions: Partner has no contractual restrictions on data redistribution; partner may monetize data beyond agreed scope
uncertainty_note: Tree node D.1.1 is a standard disclosure node; confidence in applicability is high based on common third-party data sharing risks

title: Data Misuse for Unintended Purposes
description: Partner may use the aggregated analytics data for purposes beyond app funding (e.g., building user profiles, selling to advertisers, training AI models) without user consent.
assumptions: Partner has broad data usage rights; user expectations of limited data use are not enforced
uncertainty_note: U.1.1 is a standard usurpation node; this threat is grounded in common third-party analytics misuse patterns

title: Regulatory Non-Compliance in Data Sharing
description: Partner may fail to comply with privacy regulations (GDPR, CCPA, etc.) regarding data collection, processing, or retention of the shared analytics data.
assumptions: Partner operates across multiple jurisdictions; data may be subject to various privacy laws
uncertainty_note: Nc.1.1 is a standard non-compliance node; applicability depends on partner's jurisdiction and data handling practices

title: Re-identification Risk from Aggregated Data
description: Even though data is aggregated, patterns in usage/engagement analytics may allow the partner to re-identify individual users through cross-referencing with other datasets.
assumptions: Aggregation may not be sufficient; partner may have access to additional data sources for correlation
uncertainty_note: L.1.1 is a standard linkability node; confidence is moderate as aggregation level and de-identification techniques are not specified

title: Location data linkability to child identity
description: The child's location data sent in the check-in/SOS message can be linked to their identity, potentially enabling tracking of movement patterns and correlating with other personal data.
assumptions: The system stores or logs the check-in messages with identifiable information
uncertainty_note: Using generic L.1.1 node as specific tree node not provided in context

title: Child identifiability through SOS message
description: The SOS/check-in message inherently identifies the child as the sender, making them identifiable to the parent and potentially to any system that processes the message.
assumptions: The message contains or is associated with the child's identity
uncertainty_note: Using generic I.1.1 node as specific tree node not provided in context

title: Location data disclosure to unauthorized parties
description: The child's current location data could be disclosed to unauthorized parties if the Mobile App Backend is compromised or if the data is transmitted insecurely.
assumptions: The data flow is not adequately protected or the backend has insufficient access controls
uncertainty_note: Using generic D.1.1 node as specific tree node not provided in context

title: Child identity usurpation in SOS message
description: An attacker could impersonate the child to send a false SOS message with fabricated location data, potentially causing emergency response to be misdirected.
assumptions: The system lacks proper authentication or the child's device can be compromised
uncertainty_note: Using generic U.1.1 node as specific tree node not provided in context
